rubric_definition: After you make the edit that one reviewer is asking for, does the other reviewer's comment still stand? If it is discharged too, the two findings are one defect; if it survives, they are different defects that share a location. If a reviewer offers two alternative fixes, either one discharging the other comment makes it one defect. Contradictory prescriptions to the same lines are different defects, because no single edit satisfies both.
evidence: Both findings say `touchUpdatedAt`'s monotonic `updatedAt: { lt: at }` where-clause has no direct unit test (only indirect/mocked coverage via the controller spec); adding those unit tests in document.service.spec.ts discharges both comments.

panel.summary: `touchUpdatedAt`'s monotonic guard (`where: { updatedAt: { lt: at } }`) is untested — the idempotency/out-of-order property the code and webhook rely on is unverified
panel.evidence: document.service.ts adds `touchUpdatedAt` whose whole point (per its docstring) is that it only moves time forward and no-ops on missing rows. document.service.spec.ts (new in this diff) tests only `updateDocument`; it never constructs a service with an `updateMany` mock. The controller spec mocks `touchUpdatedAt` away entirely (yorkie-event.controller.spec.ts:9-12), so no test would catch dropping the `lt` filter and letting an out-of-order/duplicate webhook move `updatedAt` backwards.

coderabbit.finding_key: packages/backend/src/document/document.service.spec.ts::add direct unit tests for `touchupdatedat` monotonic semantics.
coderabbit.summary: Add direct unit tests for `touchUpdatedAt` monotonic semantics.
coderabbit.evidence: **Add direct unit tests for `touchUpdatedAt` monotonic semantics.** The `updateDocument` tests are solid, but `touchUpdatedAt` — the critical monotonic update method — is only exercised indirectly through the controller spec. Direct unit tests would verify the `updateMany` where-clause (`updatedAt: { lt: at }`) and the returned count, covering edge cases like older timestamps (no-op), equal timestamps (no-op), and missing documents (count 0). As per coding guidelines, tests should be written for critical business logic and edge cases.
